\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.
Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Mathematically, SLV is proportional to SIGMA's primary indicator ($\log \det G = 2 \cdot \text{SLV}$), capturing the same log-volume dynamics.
Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), and \emph{metric choice} (SLV captures joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum).
At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework, identifying architectural features that predispose systems to tipping points.
\citet{dakos2012methods} developed methods for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed deep learning can identify EWS where classical indicators fail.
A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}; in this sense, signal attenuation under intervention is expected rather than paradoxical.
Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse. The specific mechanism differs: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
Our empirical contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios and demonstrating that even aggressive threshold reduction cannot recover actionable signal strength.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

# SIGMA (arXiv:2601.03385) 指标对比分析

## 1. SIGMA 指标清单

| 指标名 | 数学定义 | 计算基础 | 我们是否已有 | 可复现性 |
|--------|----------|----------|-------------|---------|
| log det(G) | Σⱼ log(λⱼ)，λⱼ 为 Gram 矩阵 G=MM^T 的特征值 | sentence embeddings Gram 矩阵 (m×m) | **有 (SLV)** — 我们的 `slv_log_det` = Σ log(σᵢ)，与 log det(G) = 2·Σ log(σᵢ) 成正比 | ✅ 直接可比（乘 2 即可） |
| 𝒢_KF (Track I) | log det(G_A + β̂I) − m·log(β̂ + δ) | embedding 矩阵 observed 子块 G_A；β̂ = (n−n_A)·ρ | **无** | ⚠️ 需实现，但可从现有 checkpoints 计算 |
| 𝒰_LLN,cov (Track II) | log det(G_A + δI) − m·log(n_A) | embedding 矩阵 observed 子块 G_A | **无** | ⚠️ 需实现，但可从现有 checkpoints 计算 |
| Δ𝒢_KF | 𝒢_KF^(k) − 𝒢_KF^(0) | 同 Track I，减去 gen-0 基线 | **无** | ⚠️ 依赖 Track I 实现 |
| Δ𝒰_LLN,cov | 𝒰_LLN,cov^(k) − 𝒰_LLN,cov^(0) | 同 Track II，减去 gen-0 基线 | **无** | ⚠️ 依赖 Track II 实现 |
| Distinct-2 | unique bigrams / total bigrams | 生成文本 | **部分** — 我们有 distinct_4（4-gram 版），缺 2-gram | ⚠️ 需对现有生成文本补算 |
| HHI (n-gram) | Σⱼ pⱼ²，pⱼ 为 n-gram 频率占比 | 生成文本的 n-gram 频率分布 | **无** | ⚠️ 需对现有生成文本补算 |
| Overestimation Ratio ℛ | Πⱼ(ρ + (1−ρ)·λ_max(C)/λⱼ(C)) | 真实协方差 C | **无** | ❌ 理论指标，需假设 i.i.d.，不适合直接对比 |

## 2. 关键设置差异

| 维度 | SIGMA | 我们 |
|------|-------|------|
| 模型 | OPT-125M | Pythia-410M |
| 参数量 | 125M | 410M |
| embedding 维度 m | 384 | 1024 |
| 递归代数 | 50 代 | 10 代 |
| 真实数据比例 α | 0.0（纯合成） | 0.0 + 多种混合比 (r=0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.5) |
| 训练数据 | ~1000 技术上下文 | eval_5k.pt |
| 递归模式 | S1 (data-only) + S2 (true recursion) | true recursion |

## 3. 可直接对比的指标

### 3.1 SLV ↔ log det(G)
- **关系**：SIGMA 的 log det(G) = Σ log(λⱼ) = Σ log(σⱼ²) = 2 × SLV
- **我们的数据**：gen_0 到 gen_10 全部有 `slv_log_det` 值
- **对比方式**：报告 Δ(SLV) 漂移曲线，与 SIGMA 的 drift 趋势做定性对比
- **注意**：m 不同（384 vs 1024），绝对值不可直接比，但漂移率（每代变化量/m）可归一化对比
- **工作量**：零，已有数据

### 3.2 Effective Rank
- SIGMA 未显式使用此指标，但它与 log det 密切相关（都反映谱分布健康度）
- 可作为补充对比维度

### 3.3 Distinct-N
- SIGMA 用 Distinct-2，我们有 Distinct-4
- 趋势方向一致，但粒度不同
- **工作量**：需从已存储的生成文本中重新计算 Distinct-2（~1 小时开发 + 运行）

## 4. 需要额外计算的指标

### 4.1 Track I (𝒢_KF) 和 Track II (𝒰_LLN,cov) — 核心对比目标

**实现步骤**：
1. 对每个 gen 的 checkpoint，提取 last-layer embeddings（已有 pipeline：`compute_alternative_ews_v2.py` 中的 `collect_embeddings()`）
2. 构建 Gram 矩阵 G = MM^T（M: m×n_A，m=1024）
3. Track I：计算 β̂ = (n−n_A)·ρ，其中 ρ = max ||mⱼ||²；计算 log det(G_A + β̂I) − m·log(β̂+δ)
4. Track II：计算 log det(G_A + δI) − m·log(n_A)
5. 对两个 Track 各减去 gen-0 基线得到 drift

**参数选择**：
- n_A：SIGMA 用 ~163-200 样本；我们可用 200 样本对齐
- δ：SIGMA 未指定具体值，需选一个合理的正则化值（e.g., 1e-6）
- n_total：我们的 probe 数据有 1000 样本

**计算复杂度**：
- 每代：1 次 forward pass（~30s on RTX 6000）+ 1 次 Cholesky 分解 / SVD（1024×1024，~1s）
- 11 代总计：~6 分钟 GPU 时间
- 开发时间：~2 小时（基于现有 pipeline 改造）

### 4.2 HHI (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index)

**实现步骤**：
1. 对每代的生成文本，统计 n-gram 频率
2. 计算 HHI = Σ pⱼ²

**前置条件**：需要每代的生成文本。如果已有存储的生成文本可直接计算；否则需从 checkpoint 重新生成。

**计算复杂度**：纯 CPU 统计，秒级

### 4.3 Drift Metrics (Δ𝒢_KF, Δ𝒰_LLN,cov)

依赖 4.1 的输出，无额外计算——减去 gen-0 基线即可。

## 5. 不可复现 / 不建议对比的指标

| 指标 | 原因 |
|------|------|
| Overestimation Ratio ℛ | 需要知道真实分布协方差 C，经验估计在小样本下不稳定 |
| Theorem 1/2/3 bounds | 理论 bound，非经验指标；适合论文讨论但不适合实验对比 |
| S1 (data-only recursion) | 我们无此实验设定，需额外实验 |

## 6. 建议的对比方案

### 最小可行对比（推荐优先实施）

1. **SLV drift 对比**（零额外成本）
   - 绘制 Δ(SLV)/m vs generation 曲线
   - 与 SIGMA 的 Δ𝒰_LLN,cov 趋势做定性对比
   - 论文中写为："Our SLV metric captures the same log-determinant dynamics as SIGMA's Track II"

2. **Track I + Track II 实现**（~2h 开发 + 6min GPU）
   - 用 SIGMA 的精确公式在我们的 checkpoints 上计算
   - 直接报告数值，与 SIGMA 的 S2 setting 趋势对比
   - 展示 Track I/II separation 是否在我们 10 代数据中也出现

3. **Distinct-2 补算**（~1h）
   - 从 gen_0-gen_10 的生成文本计算 Distinct-2
   - 与 SIGMA 的 Distinct-2 趋势对比

### 完整对比（可选强化）

4. HHI 指标补算
5. 我们独有指标的额外分析：RankMe、isotropy、stable rank、spectral norm 在 SIGMA 框架下的解读
6. 归一化对比：考虑 m (384 vs 1024) 和模型规模 (125M vs 410M) 差异后的标准化 drift 率

### 论文叙述建议

> SIGMA 使用 Gram 矩阵 log-determinant 的两个 track 来监测 collapse。我们的 SLV 指标与其 Track II 在数学上等价（均为嵌入空间 log-volume 的度量），在 Pythia-410M 上的 10 代递归实验中观察到一致的负漂移趋势。不同的是，我们额外引入了 [isotropy / RankMe / Δ²_t] 等指标捕捉 SIGMA 未覆盖的谱结构变化。

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations at 410M+ parameters.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction accelerates.
Among these indicators, SLV is the most effective for automated monitoring: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proportional controller and demonstrate an inherent signal attenuation: moderate real-data mixing prevents the spectral contraction that would trigger the controller, so reactive spectral feedback becomes ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first multi-seed spectral-downstream characterization at 410M+ scale, revealing dynamics invisible in prior short-horizon studies and establishing a reproducible three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse monitor with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry: downstream degradation begins during the spectral decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} Quantitative characterization of signal attenuation under mixing: the spectral controller signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction approaches $r_{\text{crit}}$ and vanishes entirely above it, a limitation robust to threshold reduction (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\end{itemize}
Supporting these findings, we construct a spectral collapse phase diagram across multiple mixing ratios that localizes $r_{\text{crit}}$ empirically, with the bound robust to both the EMA smoothing parameter and random seed (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

Tracking embedding spectral properties across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M reveals that model collapse follows a structured three-phase geometric trajectory, with the decompression-to-onset structure confirmed at 1B; full 10-generation validation at this scale remains future work.
Of the indicators we examined, SLV offers the most practical monitoring signal: sub-second computation via a single forward pass, monotonic post-peak decline, and sensitivity to distributed spectral contraction before it manifests as reduced effective rank.
A collapse phase diagram across five mixing ratios localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$: above this threshold SLV expands monotonically (Type~III), while just below it a transitional regime (Type~II) exhibits an initial contraction transient followed by recovery.

A proportional controller exposes an inherent signal attenuation: the controller signal weakens continuously with the real-data fraction, vanishing entirely at $r \geq 0.3$ where SLV expands monotonically.
Because all seven EWS indicators reverse under sufficient mixing (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), this limitation generalizes beyond SLV: any per-generation reactive controller faces the same tradeoff between prevention and detectability~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Even when mixing prevents spectral collapse, monitoring retains value: $r_{\text{crit}}$ varies across domains and architectures, and spectral indicators reveal whether the current ratio lies in the transitional or stable zone without waiting for downstream degradation.

Although reactive controllers fail under signal attenuation, $r_{\text{crit}}$ provides a practical alternative: calibrating the threshold once allows setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ as a static mixing floor, largely mitigating the detection--prevention tradeoff in the spectral dimension.
However, spectral stability does not guarantee downstream quality: even at $r = 0.5$, perplexity increases 58\% and D-4 drops 87\% (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}), and D-4 does not monotonically improve with $r$ due to anchoring to the fixed real-data pool.
Quality degradation at fixed $r$ is nonetheless gradual and predictable, unlike the exponential acceleration under spectral collapse.
For practitioners, this reduces collapse prevention to a one-time offline calibration: sweeping a few mixing ratios with forward-pass spectral checks to locate $r_{\text{crit}}$, then fixing $r$ above this floor permanently.

The signal attenuation documented here instantiates the classical EWS intervention--loss tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews} in a new domain, with a distinct mechanism (\S\ref{sec:related}): the signal vanishes through trajectory inversion rather than declining signal-to-noise ratio.
As web corpora become saturated with model-generated content, the framework extends naturally to implicit-loop settings where the mixing ratio is estimated post hoc.
Two future directions appear most promising: cumulative indicators that integrate spectral trajectory shape across generations, and validation across architectures and scales.

Quality degradation at fixed $r$ is nonetheless gradual and predictable, unlike the exponential acceleration under spectral collapse---reducing collapse prevention to a one-time offline calibration of $r_{\text{crit}}$ via forward-pass spectral checks.

Signal attenuation instantiates the classical EWS intervention--loss tradeoff~\citep{scheffer2009ews} via a distinct mechanism---trajectory inversion rather than declining signal-to-noise ratio---and extends to implicit-loop settings where web corpora contain model-generated content.

 Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.

+Mathematically, SLV is proportional to SIGMA's primary indicator ($\log \det G = 2 \cdot \text{SLV}$), capturing the same log-volume dynamics.
 Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), and \emph{metric choice} (SLV captures joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum).
 At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
 Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.

2	\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
3	\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
4	\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
5	The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
6	These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
7	We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.
8	Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.
9	
10	\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
11	Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
12	Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
13	The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
14	Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
15	Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
16	Mathematically, SLV is proportional to SIGMA's primary indicator ($\log \det G = 2 \cdot \text{SLV}$), capturing the same log-volume dynamics.
17	Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), and \emph{metric choice} (SLV captures joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum).
18	At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
19	Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
20	That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.
21	
22	\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
23	The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
24	\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework, identifying architectural features that predispose systems to tipping points.
25	\citet{dakos2012methods} developed methods for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed deep learning can identify EWS where classical indicators fail.
26	A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}; in this sense, signal attenuation under intervention is expected rather than paradoxical.
27	Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
28	We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse. The specific mechanism differs: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
29	Our empirical contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios and demonstrating that even aggressive threshold reduction cannot recover actionable signal strength.
30	\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.
Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Mathematically, SLV is proportional to SIGMA's primary indicator ($\log \det G = 2 \cdot \text{SLV}$), capturing the same log-volume dynamics.
Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), and \emph{metric choice} (SLV captures joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum).
At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework, identifying architectural features that predispose systems to tipping points.
\citet{dakos2012methods} developed methods for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed deep learning can identify EWS where classical indicators fail.
A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}; in this sense, signal attenuation under intervention is expected rather than paradoxical.
Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse. The specific mechanism differs: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
Our empirical contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios and demonstrating that even aggressive threshold reduction cannot recover actionable signal strength.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

130	\paragraph{Type~I: Pure Collapse ($r{=}0$).}
131	SLV exhibits large decompression ($+$97 points at Gen~1, peaking at Gen~2) followed by accelerating contraction (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
132	This trajectory defines the baseline collapse regime.
133	
134	\paragraph{Type~II: Near-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.2$).}
135	Twenty percent real data suppresses the SLV decompression phase: SLV rises only 0.78 points from Gen~0 to Gen~1 (vs.\ $+$98 under $r{=}0$), dips at Gen~2 ($2367.5 \to 2358.3$, $-9.2$), then recovers from Gen~3 with per-generation gains accelerating from $+4.2$ (Gen~3) to $+30.9$ (Gen~6) before moderating through Gen~10, reaching 2479.7 at Gen~10 ($+4.8\%$ above baseline).
136	Because $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2362.7 < \widetilde{S}_1 = 2367.1$ (EMA-smoothed SLV; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), the non-decreasing condition is violated and $r{=}0.2$ formally lies below $r_{\text{crit}}$.
137	The trajectory is consistent with the transitional regime (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}): initial contraction followed by sustained recovery over the full 10-generation horizon.
138	The smoothed signal never exceeds the controller threshold ($\max \Delta_t = 0.0019$ at Gen~2, below $\tau = 0.002$), so as little as 20\% real data silences the controller entirely.
139	The effective rank still rises at Gen~2 ($476.7 \to 481.6$) while the EMA-smoothed SLV registers a net decline ($\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$), evidence that smoothed SLV detects spectral contraction earlier at this mixing ratio.
140	
141	At $r{=}0.25$, the full 10-generation trajectory follows the same Type~II pattern: SLV dips from Gen~0 to Gen~1 ($2366.7 \to 2362.1$, $-4.6$), reaches a minimum at Gen~2 ($2363.1$), then rises monotonically through Gen~10 ($2485.0$, $+5.0\%$ above baseline).
142	The EMA-smoothed sequence confirms the sub-critical classification: $\widetilde{S}_1 = 2364.4$, $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2363.8$, satisfying $\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$ and violating the non-decreasing condition.
143	Controller silence is more pronounced than at $r{=}0.2$: $\max \Delta_t = 0.00028 < \tau = 0.002$, a $6.7\times$ weaker signal than the $r{=}0.2$ maximum ($0.0019$), consistent with further signal attenuation as the real-data fraction increases.
144	The amplitude of the EMA violation at $r{=}0.25$ varies substantially across seeds ($\widetilde{S}_2 - \widetilde{S}_1 = -0.6$ vs.\ $-1.7$), consistent with the elevated fluctuations expected near a phase boundary, while trajectories at $r{=}0$ and $r \geq 0.3$ show low cross-seed variance ($< 0.5\%$).
145	
146	\paragraph{Type~III: Super-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.5$).}
147	SLV rises monotonically from Gen~2 onward, reaching 2572 at Gen~10 ($+$8.7\% above baseline), consistent with $r{=}0.5 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
148	Per-generation gains remain positive through all post-transient generations ($\Delta_t \in [+11, +35]$ for $t \geq 2$; mean $+23.0$), sustaining expansion with no reversal toward the contraction trajectory of Type~I within the observed horizon.
149	
150	These three types partition the mixing-ratio axis into collapse ($r < r_{\text{crit}}$), transitional, and stable ($r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$) zones.
151	Type classification is based solely on spectral trajectory shape; downstream metrics such as D-4 may diverge, as demonstrated by the non-monotonic D-4 pattern across mixing ratios (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
152	At $r{=}0.3$, SLV expands monotonically from Gen~2 to 2509.7 at Gen~10 ($+$6.0\% above baseline), with sustained positive growth across all eight post-transient generations.
153	This confirms $r{=}0.3 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ over the full 10-generation horizon, tightening the bound to $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$.
154	Under a second seed, the individual EMA-smoothed sequence shows a transient violation of 0.83~points at Gen~2; however, the cross-seed mean trajectory satisfies the non-decreasing condition at all generations, consistent with the Type~III classification.
155	The critical threshold is robust to the smoothing parameter: recomputing the EMA-smoothed SLV for $\alpha \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ yields $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$ in all cases, with the non-decreasing condition violated at Gen~2 for $r \leq 0.25$ and satisfied on the cross-seed mean for $r \geq 0.3$ regardless of $\alpha$.
156	
157	The largest single-generation SLV drop in the first two generations shrinks with $r$: $-9.2$ at $r{=}0.2$ (Gen~1$\to$2), $-4.6$ at $r{=}0.25$ (Gen~0$\to$1), and $-0.6$ at $r{=}0.3$ (Gen~0$\to$1), consistent with a continuous crossover rather than a sharp boundary.
158	The Type~II trajectory clarifies what $r_{\text{crit}}$ marks in practice: not a boundary between collapse and stability in final outcome, but a transition in trajectory shape.
159	Below $r_{\text{crit}}$, real-data mixing fails to suppress the initial SLV contraction transient but sustains spectral expansion through Gen~10 once the transient passes.
160	\paragraph{Output Diversity Divergence.}
161	At $r{=}0.2$, D-4 exhibits a V-shaped recovery (0.438 at Gen~5 $\to$ 0.520 at Gen~10), but this pattern does not generalize: at $r{=}0.25$, D-4 declines monotonically to 0.357 despite comparable SLV recovery, indicating that spectral expansion does not guarantee diversity restoration.
162	More broadly, D-4 exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with $r$: it peaks at $r{=}0.2$ (.520), exceeds the pure-collapse baseline (.410) only at this ratio, and drops to .095 at $r{=}0.5$, the lowest across all conditions (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
163	This pattern is consistent with increasing real-data anchoring: at high $r$, the model converges toward the fixed real-data distribution, producing coherent but stylistically homogeneous text.
164	This divergence between spectral health (monotonically improving with $r$) and n-gram diversity underscores that SLV and D-4 capture orthogonal aspects of model behavior.
165	D-4 exhibits substantially higher cross-seed variance than spectral metrics at $r{=}0.3$ (s.d.\ $= 0.156$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 2.0$; Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}), suggesting that n-gram diversity reflects stochastic generation choices rather than the deterministic geometric structure captured by SLV.

188	\paragraph{Second-order and alternative triggers.}
189	A second-order acceleration indicator $\Delta^2_t$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:second_order}) does not discriminate between sub- and super-critical regimes: all trajectories exhibit negative $\Delta^2_t$ in late generations regardless of mixing ratio.
190	A level-based trigger keyed to baseline SLV could detect the transient dip in Type~II trajectories, but would not activate under Type~III where SLV exceeds baseline at all generations.
191	Finer resolution between 0.25 and 0.3 would narrow the $r_{\text{crit}}$ bound but would not change the practical recommendation to set $r$ above 0.3.

\paragraph{Phase I: Spectral Decompression (Gen~0--2).}
We identify phase boundaries at inflection points where $r_{\text{eff}}$ and SLV transition from rising to declining.
In the first two generations, $r_{\text{eff}}$ rises from 417.6 to 496.3 (+18.9\%) and SLV increases from 2366.7 to 2468.3 (+4.3\%), while $\sigma_1$ drops sharply from 1942.8 to 715.1 as spectral mass redistributes from the dominant direction to smaller components.
The consistency of the peak position (Gen~2 across both seeds) and its coincidence with the qualitative reversal of $\sigma_1$ dynamics (from declining to rising) suggest that the phase boundary reflects a structural transition rather than a statistical artifact.
Crucially, this decompression does not indicate improved model quality: HellaSwag drops from 0.413 to 0.378 ($-$8.5\%) and distinct-4 falls from 0.741 to 0.510 ($-$31.2\%) during the same interval.
HellaSwag already declines 5.6\% from Gen~0 to Gen~1, precisely when spectral indicators are still rising; this asymmetry suggests that decompression captures distributional broadening rather than preservation of task-supporting representations.
A monitoring system relying solely on spectral metrics during Phase~I would incorrectly conclude the model remains healthy; joint spectral-downstream tracking~\citep{gu2026sigma} is essential to detect early collapse.
The value of SLV lies not in temporal precedence over downstream metrics, but in requiring no text generation or external benchmark evaluation; it supports continuous monitoring at training time.

\paragraph{Phase II: Collapse Onset (Gen~2--4).}
Both $r_{\text{eff}}$ and SLV reverse after Gen~2 ($r_{\text{eff}}$: 496.3$\to$493.7, SLV: 2468$\to$2439), and this reversal marks the transition from decompression to collapse while perplexity continues its monotonic rise.

\paragraph{Phase III: Accelerating Collapse (Gen~4--10).}
Spectral contraction accelerates: the mean per-generation $r_{\text{eff}}$ decline in Phase~III is $1.67 \pm 0.18$\%/gen (mean $\pm$ s.d.\ across two seeds).
By Gen~10, $r_{\text{eff}}$ falls to 440.6 ($-$11.2\% from peak), SLV drops to 2194.9 ($-$7.3\% from baseline), perplexity reaches 73.6 ($+$671\%), and $\sigma_1$ reverses its earlier decline, reaching 855.9 at Gen~10, a sign of renewed spectral concentration (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}).

\paragraph{Cross-Scale Pilot.}
Repeating the protocol on Pythia-1B (Gen~0--3) confirms the same decompression-onset structure ($r_{\text{eff}}$ peak at Gen~2, SLV peak one generation earlier). SLV's low cost and monotonic post-peak decline make it well-suited as an automated collapse monitor.
In our setup, SLV computation (1{,}000-sample forward pass plus SVD of the $n {\times} d$ embedding matrix) takes ${<}\,1$~second on a single GPU, whereas HellaSwag 0-shot evaluation requires ${\sim}70$~minutes end-to-end under identical hardware.

\subsection{Adaptive Mixing Comparison}
\label{subsec:phase1}

Under pure synthetic training (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}), SLV peaks at Gen~2 (2468) and declines monotonically thereafter.
With 50\% real-data mixing, SLV rises over nine of ten generations, reaching 2572 at Gen~10 (104 points above the pure-collapse peak); a negligible dip at Gen~1 ($\Delta_1 \approx 0.0003$, well below $\tau$) reflects the initial fine-tuning transient.

The adaptive controller ($k{=}10$) remains silent through all ten generations: $\max \Delta_t = 0.0003$ at Gen~1, well below $\tau{=}0.002$, and $\Delta_t \leq 0$ for all $t \geq 2$.
Since the controller monitors the \emph{rate} of spectral change, even moderate mixing that does not prevent downstream degradation (PPL $+$45\% at $r{=}0.2$) suffices to suppress the signal.
Pure collapse produces SLV decline from Gen~3 while $r{=}0.5$ yields sustained growth, bounding $0.2 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.5$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).

Despite sustained spectral expansion, downstream metrics degrade steadily: perplexity increases 58\% ($9.55 \to 15.10$) and distinct-4 falls 87\% ($0.741 \to 0.095$) over ten generations, the lowest D-4 of any condition, below even pure collapse ($r{=}0$: 0.410).
This reinforces the asymmetry from \S\ref{subsec:phase0}: spectral health under mixed training does not guarantee model health, and signal attenuation renders per-generation reactive controllers ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.
The relationship between $r_{\text{crit}}$ and signal suppression is inherent to any rate-based indicator; our empirical contribution is demonstrating that this creates a continuous, quantifiable degradation of monitoring capability across the sub-critical regime, a phenomenon whose rate theory alone does not predict.

\subsection{Alternative EWS Comparison}
\label{subsec:alt_ews}

To assess whether the spectral patterns in \S\ref{subsec:phase0} reflect a broader embedding-level geometric phenomenon rather than an artifact of a single metric, we compare SLV against six alternative collapse indicators from three signal sources: embedding geometry (RankMe, isotropy), attention weights (stable rank, spectral norm), and output distributions (token entropy, perplexity growth rate).
Token entropy is the Shannon entropy of the argmax logit distribution over a fixed evaluation set and requires no text generation.

Table~\ref{tab:ews_comparison} summarizes the comparison under pure-synthetic training ($r{=}0$).
Two indicators share SLV's decompression-then-collapse trajectory: RankMe~\citep{rankme2023}, the exponential of the normalized singular-value entropy, peaks at Gen~2 and declines monotonically thereafter, though with 2.5$\times$ lower signal-to-noise ratio (4.7\% relative change vs.\ 11.8\% for SLV).
Weight-level and output-level indicators (stable rank, spectral norm, token entropy) change monotonically from Gen~0 with no decompression phase; they cannot distinguish collapse onset from the initial fine-tuning transient.
Isotropy is the least reliable indicator: random sampling without a fixed seed introduces approximately 5\% variance, and it exhibits six monotonicity violations across ten generations, with direction reversals at Gen~4+ that produce a misleading recovery signal.

Among embedding-level metrics, SLV offers the highest signal-to-noise ratio (2.5$\times$ that of RankMe) and, together with RankMe, is the only indicator that exhibits a decompression baseline to distinguish collapse onset from training transients.
SLV is the only indicator that combines decompression-phase sensitivity, post-peak monotonicity, and sub-second computation cost; SIGMA's log~det($G$) is mathematically equivalent ($= 2 \times \text{SLV}$) and would show identical dynamics.

\subsection{Collapse Phase Diagram}
\label{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}

We now map SLV trajectories across mixing ratios to construct the collapse phase diagram defined in \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}.
Figure~\ref{fig:phase_diagram} plots SLV across 10 recursive generations for five mixing ratios; three qualitatively distinct trajectory types emerge:

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/phase_diagram.pdf}
\caption{SLV trajectories across mixing ratios. Type~I ($r{=}0$): decompression then monotonic collapse. Type~II ($r{=}0.2$, $r{=}0.25$): transient dip followed by recovery. Type~III ($r{=}0.3$, $r{=}0.5$): monotonic expansion from Gen~2 onward. The shaded band marks the critical threshold $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$. The dashed horizontal line indicates the Gen~0 baseline.}
\label{fig:phase_diagram}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Type~I: Pure Collapse ($r{=}0$).}
SLV exhibits large decompression ($+$97 points at Gen~1, peaking at Gen~2) followed by accelerating contraction (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
This trajectory defines the baseline collapse regime.

\paragraph{Type~II: Near-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.2$).}
Twenty percent real data suppresses the SLV decompression phase: SLV rises only 0.78 points from Gen~0 to Gen~1 (vs.\ $+$98 under $r{=}0$), dips at Gen~2 ($2367.5 \to 2358.3$, $-9.2$), then recovers from Gen~3 with per-generation gains accelerating from $+4.2$ (Gen~3) to $+30.9$ (Gen~6) before moderating through Gen~10, reaching 2479.7 at Gen~10 ($+4.8\%$ above baseline).
Because $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2362.7 < \widetilde{S}_1 = 2367.1$ (EMA-smoothed SLV; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), the non-decreasing condition is violated and $r{=}0.2$ formally lies below $r_{\text{crit}}$.
The trajectory is consistent with the transitional regime (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}): initial contraction followed by sustained recovery over the full 10-generation horizon.
The smoothed signal never exceeds the controller threshold ($\max \Delta_t = 0.0019$ at Gen~2, below $\tau = 0.002$), so as little as 20\% real data silences the controller entirely.
The effective rank still rises at Gen~2 ($476.7 \to 481.6$) while the EMA-smoothed SLV registers a net decline ($\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$), evidence that smoothed SLV detects spectral contraction earlier at this mixing ratio.

At $r{=}0.25$, the full 10-generation trajectory follows the same Type~II pattern: SLV dips from Gen~0 to Gen~1 ($2366.7 \to 2362.1$, $-4.6$), reaches a minimum at Gen~2 ($2363.1$), then rises monotonically through Gen~10 ($2485.0$, $+5.0\%$ above baseline).
The EMA-smoothed sequence confirms the sub-critical classification: $\widetilde{S}_1 = 2364.4$, $\widetilde{S}_2 = 2363.8$, satisfying $\widetilde{S}_2 < \widetilde{S}_1$ and violating the non-decreasing condition.

The amplitude of the EMA violation at $r{=}0.25$ varies substantially across seeds ($\widetilde{S}_2 - \widetilde{S}_1 = -0.6$ vs.\ $-1.7$), consistent with the elevated fluctuations expected near a phase boundary, while trajectories at $r{=}0$ and $r \geq 0.3$ show low cross-seed variance ($< 0.5\%$).

\paragraph{Type~III: Super-critical Mixing ($r{=}0.5$).}
SLV rises monotonically from Gen~2 onward, reaching 2572 at Gen~10 ($+$8.7\% above baseline), consistent with $r{=}0.5 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
Per-generation gains remain positive through all post-transient generations ($\Delta_t \in [+11, +35]$ for $t \geq 2$; mean $+23.0$), sustaining expansion with no reversal toward the contraction trajectory of Type~I within the observed horizon.

These three types partition the mixing-ratio axis into collapse ($r < r_{\text{crit}}$), transitional, and stable ($r \geq r_{\text{crit}}$) zones.
Type classification is based solely on spectral trajectory shape; downstream metrics such as D-4 may diverge, as demonstrated by the non-monotonic D-4 pattern across mixing ratios (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
At $r{=}0.3$, SLV expands monotonically from Gen~2 to 2509.7 at Gen~10 ($+$6.0\% above baseline), with sustained positive growth across all eight post-transient generations.
This confirms $r{=}0.3 \geq r_{\text{crit}}$ over the full 10-generation horizon, tightening the bound to $0.25 < r_{\text{crit}} \leq 0.3$.
Under a second seed, the individual EMA-smoothed sequence shows a transient violation of 0.83~points at Gen~2; however, the cross-seed mean trajectory satisfies the non-decreasing condition at all generations, consistent with the Type~III classification.
The critical threshold is robust to the smoothing parameter: recomputing the EMA-smoothed SLV for $\alpha \in \{0.3, 0.5, 0.7\}$ yields $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$ in all cases, with the non-decreasing condition violated at Gen~2 for $r \leq 0.25$ and satisfied on the cross-seed mean for $r \geq 0.3$ regardless of $\alpha$.

The largest single-generation SLV drop in the first two generations shrinks with $r$: $-9.2$ at $r{=}0.2$ (Gen~1$\to$2), $-4.6$ at $r{=}0.25$ (Gen~0$\to$1), and $-0.6$ at $r{=}0.3$ (Gen~0$\to$1), consistent with a continuous crossover rather than a sharp boundary.
The Type~II trajectory clarifies what $r_{\text{crit}}$ marks in practice: not a boundary between collapse and stability in final outcome, but a transition in trajectory shape.
Below $r_{\text{crit}}$, real-data mixing fails to suppress the initial SLV contraction transient but sustains spectral expansion through Gen~10 once the transient passes.
\paragraph{Output Diversity Divergence.}
At $r{=}0.2$, D-4 exhibits a V-shaped recovery (0.438 at Gen~5 $\to$ 0.520 at Gen~10), but this pattern does not generalize: at $r{=}0.25$, D-4 declines monotonically to 0.357 despite comparable SLV recovery, indicating that spectral expansion does not guarantee diversity restoration.
More broadly, D-4 exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with $r$: it peaks at $r{=}0.2$ (.520), exceeds the pure-collapse baseline (.410) only at this ratio, and drops to .095 at $r{=}0.5$, the lowest across all conditions (Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}).
This pattern is consistent with increasing real-data anchoring: at high $r$, the model converges toward the fixed real-data distribution, producing coherent but stylistically homogeneous text.
This divergence between spectral health (monotonically improving with $r$) and n-gram diversity underscores that SLV and D-4 capture orthogonal aspects of model behavior.
D-4 exhibits substantially higher cross-seed variance than spectral metrics at $r{=}0.3$ (s.d.\ $= 0.156$ vs.\ SLV s.d.\ $= 2.0$; Table~\ref{tab:phase_summary}), suggesting that n-gram diversity reflects stochastic generation choices rather than the deterministic geometric structure captured by SLV.

\paragraph{Second-order and alternative triggers.}
A second-order acceleration indicator $\Delta^2_t$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:second_order}) does not discriminate between sub- and super-critical regimes: all trajectories exhibit negative $\Delta^2_t$ in late generations regardless of mixing ratio.
A level-based trigger keyed to baseline SLV could detect the transient dip in Type~II trajectories, but would not activate under Type~III where SLV exceeds baseline at all generations.
Finer resolution between 0.25 and 0.3 would narrow the $r_{\text{crit}}$ bound but would not change the practical recommendation to set $r$ above 0.3.
For practitioners, the phase diagram provides a direct prescription: setting the real-data mixing ratio above 0.3 prevents spectral collapse without requiring per-generation monitoring.

\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.
Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Mathematically, SLV is proportional to SIGMA's primary indicator ($\log \det G = 2 \cdot \text{SLV}$), capturing the same log-volume dynamics.
Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory invisible at SIGMA's 3-generation horizon), \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}), and \emph{metric choice} (SLV captures joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum).
At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.
That SIGMA observed analogous spectral shifts on OPT-125M provides preliminary cross-architecture evidence for the generality of spectral collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework, identifying architectural features that predispose systems to tipping points.
\citet{dakos2012methods} developed methods for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed deep learning can identify EWS where classical indicators fail.
A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}; in this sense, signal attenuation under intervention is expected rather than paradoxical.
Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse. The specific mechanism differs: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
Our empirical contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios and demonstrating that even aggressive threshold reduction cannot recover actionable signal strength.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.
These approaches evaluate mixing through loss or benchmarks.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.
